title: The Boomerang Nebula - the coolest place in the Universe?
caption: The Boomerang Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Boomerang Nebula, IRAS 12419-5414 · constellation Centaurus · about 5000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Faint arcs and ghostly filaments run through the smooth, bow-tie-shaped lobes of the Boomerang Nebula, a young planetary nebula 5000 light-years away in Centaurus. Planetary nebulae form when a star in the last stages of its life casts off gas. The light in the image is starlight from the central star, reflected by dust.

In 1995, Sahai and Nyman used the 15-meter Swedish ESO Submillimeter Telescope in Chile to show it is the coldest place in the Universe yet found. At -272C it is just 1 degree above absolute zero, colder even than the -270C background glow left by the Big Bang.

Keith Taylor and Mike Scarrott named it in 1980, after spotting a slight asymmetry through a ground-based telescope in Australia. Hubble's sharper view suggests the Bow tie Nebula might have fit better. Most planetary nebulae have bubble-like lobes, and this one may simply be too young to have formed them.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.32 x 1.32 arcminutes) and distance (5000 light years), the frame spans roughly 1.9 × 1.9 light-years. Its light set out about 5,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took a single 1000-second exposure through a green-yellow filter at 606 nm. With one filter, the color in the image isn't a multi-color composite.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view shows detail that ground-based telescopes could not resolve, which is why earlier observers saw only a slightly lopsided shape.

behind.people: See full credit: European Space Agency, NASA
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The bow-tie shape seems to come from a fierce wind of 500 000 kilometers per hour, blowing ultracold gas away from the dying star. The star has lost up to a thousandth of a solar mass each year for 1500 years, 10-100 times more than similar objects. That rapid expansion made the nebula so cold.
alt: A faint nebula with two smooth lobes forming a bow-tie shape around a central star, laced with thin arcs and filaments.
